t('bullet', '`SelCrossover.glsl.c` — selekcja, krzyzowanie i makro-mutacja,')
t('bullet', '`ScoreCube.glsl.c` — obliczenie baseline `cube.Score` na GPU (jedno zrodlo prawdy dla metryki).')

t('h2', '2.2 Konfiguracja przez #define i rekompilacja')
t('body', 'Parametry sa stalymi kompilacji w `Setup.glsl.c`, bo okreslaja rozmiary tablic w shaderze (np. `local_cubies[CUBIES_COUNT]`). Wartosci N, SIZE i CUBIES_COUNT sa wstrzykiwane z biezacej kostki (`SetDefineValue`) przed kompilacja. Gdy uzytkownik zmieni wymiar lub rozmiar, `CreateBuffers` wykrywa roznice (CompiledN/CompiledSize) i wyzwala rekompilacje — shader zawsze pasuje do kostki. Tu tez zdefiniowane sa progi zachowania: `MUTATION_RATIO`, `SEED_RATIO`, `WINNERS_RATIO` i `STALL_LIMIT`.')

# ---- 3 ----
t('h1', '3. Reprezentacja danych')
t('h2', '3.1 Osobnik i ruch')
t('body', 'Osobnik (chromosom) to struktura Specimen. Fitness jest przechowywany jako bity float (floatBitsToUint), dzieki czemu sortowanie bitoniczne moze porownywac go jako uint (dla nieujemnych wartosci porzadek wzorca bitowego pokrywa sie z porzadkiem liczb).')
t('code', '''struct Specimen {
    uint Fitness;            // floatBitsToUint(fitness)
    uint MovesCount;         // dlugosc najlepszego prefiksu
    uint Moves[GENES_COUNT]; // sekwencja zakodowanych ruchow
};
// Kod ruchu: angle(2b) | plane(5b) | axis(3b) | slice(reszta)
Move getMove(uint code) {
    uint angle = code & 3u;
    uint plane = (code >> 2u) & 31u;
    uint axis  = (code >> 7u) & 7u;
    uint slice = code >> 10u;
    return Move(axis, slice, plane, angle);
}''')
t('body', 'Uwaga: zaden kod nie oznacza ruchu tozsamosciowego — kazdy wzorzec bitow to realny obrot 90/180/270. Nie ma osobnikow "nic nie robiacych", co zageszcza kodowanie i upraszcza ewaluacje (patrz kara martwego ruchu, 5.4).')

t('h2', '3.2 Spakowana macierz orientacji kubika')
t('body', 'Orientacja pojedynczego kubika to macierz znakowanej permutacji N×N (kazdy wiersz ma dokladnie jeden niezerowy element ±1). Pakujemy ja do jednego uint: N wierszy po BITS_PER_ROW bitow, pole wiersza = (znak << BITS_FOR_COL) | kolumna. Tozsamosc: wiersz r koduje (kolumna=r, znak +), czyli wartosc pola = r. Ulozony kubik ma wartosc tozsamosci, a jego odleglosc L1 wynosi 0.')
t('code', '''#define BITS_FOR_COL (N <= 4 ? 2 : 3)   // bity na indeks kolumny
#define BITS_PER_ROW (BITS_FOR_COL + 1)      // + 1 bit znaku
// Dla N <= 8: N wierszy * (<=4 bity) <= 32 bity -> miesci sie w uint.''')
t('body', 'Dla N w zakresie [3, 8] cala macierz miesci sie w 32 bitach, co pozwala trzymac kubik w rejestrze i obracac go wylacznie operacjami bitowymi.')

t('h2', '3.3 Bufory GPU (kontrakt bindingow)')
t('body', 'Wszystkie bufory tworzy klasa Ssbo w stalej kolejnosci, wiec licznik bindingow daje indeksy 0–8 dokladnie tak, jak deklaruje `Setup.glsl.c`:')
t('table', [
    ['Bind', 'Bufor', 'Typ', 'Zawartosc'],
    ['0', 'Population', 'SSBO', 'Populacja rodzicow (Specimen[])'],
    ['1', 'NewPopulation', 'SSBO', 'Dzieci — wyjscie krzyzowania (ping-pong)'],
    ['2', 'Cubies', 'SSBO', 'Spakowany stan startowy (uint na kubik)'],
    ['3', 'FreeMoves', 'SSBO', 'Dozwolone kody ruchow klastra'],
    ['4', 'SolvedCubies', 'SSBO', 'Indeksy juz ulozonych kubikow'],
    ['5', 'ActiveCubies', 'SSBO', 'Indeksy kubikow aktywnego klastra'],
    ['6', 'Planes', 'UBO (std140)', 'Pary osi plaszczyzn obrotu (ivec2[])'],
    ['7', 'SeedMoves', 'SSBO', 'Sekwencje seedow per osobnik (Init/mutacja)'],
    ['8', 'ScoreBuffer', 'SSBO', 'Wynik ScoreCube — baseline cube.Score'],
], [32, 92, 78, 240])
t('body', 'Bufor Cubies jest wspoldzielony (tylko do odczytu): kazdy watek kopiuje stan startowy do prywatnej kopii roboczej i mutuje wylacznie ja — wspoldzielony bufor jest wolny od wyscigow. countSolved i countActive przekazywane sa jako uniformy (a nie przez `.length()` bufora, bo puste SSBO daje niepewne `.length()` na roznych sterownikach).')

# ---- 4 ----
t('h1', '4. Sposob dzialania — petla ewolucyjna')
t('body', 'Metoda `Gpu.ExecuteGA()` realizuje jeden przebieg algorytmu genetycznego dla biezacej kostki i zwraca najlepszego znalezionego osobnika:')
t('code', '''CreateBuffers(kostka, freeMoves)          // upload + seedy + ew. rekompilacja
UseProgram(Init); Dispatch                // Population[0]: numSeeds seedow + reszta losowa
for (gen = 0; gen < GENERATIONS_COUNT; ++gen) {
    UseProgram(evalProgram); Dispatch     // 1. fitness kazdego osobnika (z kara no-op)
    UseProgram(Sort);        Dispatch*    // 2. sortowanie bitoniczne + kara unikalnosci
    read Population[0]                     // 3. najlepszy na indeksie 0
    if (fitness < best) { best = ...;      //    zapamietaj rekord
        if (best < Score) return best; }   //    prog akceptacji (rozwiazanie)
    UseProgram(SelCrossover); Dispatch     // 4. selekcja + krzyzowanie + makro-mutacja
    parentSlot ^= 1;                       // 5. ping-pong buforow
}
return best;                              // brak poprawy: najmniej-zly REALNY ruch''')
t('body', 'Bufory populacji dzialaja w trybie ping-pong: rodzice sa zawsze pod bindingiem 0, dzieci pod bindingiem 1, a po kazdej generacji role bufow sie zamieniaja. Kluczowe: dzieki karze martwego ruchu (5.4) zwrocony best jest zawsze **realnym** ruchem zmieniajacym klaster — nawet gdy nic nie poprawia. To warunek dzialania mechanizmu stall/kop (7.3).')

t('h2', '4.1 Wymiary dispatchu: micro vs macro')
t('body', 'Ewaluacja ma dwie strategie rownoleglosci, wybierane na podstawie liczby kubikow:')
t('bullet', '**Micro** (≤ 64 kubiki): 1 watek = 1 osobnik. Kostka trzymana w prywatnej tablicy w rejestrach; watek sekwencyjnie obraca kubiki i sumuje blad. Dispatch: ceil(POP/64) blokow po 64.')
t('bullet', '**Macro** (> 64 kubiki): 1 blok (256 watkow) = 1 osobnik. Kostka w pamieci wspoldzielonej bloku; watki rownolegle obracaja kubiki, a blad liczony jest logarytmiczna redukcja rownolegla. Dispatch: POP blokow.')
t('body', 'Init i SelCrossover to zawsze 1 watek na osobnika (bloki po 64). ScoreCube to 1 watek (liczy baseline raz na klaster).')

# ---- 5 ----
t('h1', '5. Ewaluacja i metryka fitnessu')
t('h2', '5.1 Symulacja ruchu na spakowanej macierzy')
t('body', 'TurnSingleCubie sprawdza, czy dany kubik lezy w warstwie obracanej przez ruch, i jesli tak — obraca jego macierz. Przynaleznosc do warstwy wyznacza getStartCoordinate (wspolrzedna domowa kubika wzdluz osi ruchu) skorygowana o znak. Konwencja osi jest zgodna z CPU. Sam obrot to RotateMatInt na dwoch wierszach plaszczyzny obrotu (zamiana/negacja pol — jedna formula na kazdy kat 90°/180°/270°).')

t('h2', '5.2 Odleglosc L1 i miara ruchow-do-ulozenia')
t('body', 'Miara bledu kubika jest **cubieState** — nie sama odleglosc L1, lecz liczba aktywnych osi (wierszy roznych od tozsamosci) jako czlon dominujacy, dopiero potem L1 jako rozstrzygajacy remisy:')
t('code', '''uint cubieL1(uint M) {                    // Manhattan od tozsamosci; 0 <=> ulozony
    uint dist = 0u;
    for (uint r = 0u; r < uint(N); r++) {
        uint field = (M >> (r*BITS_PER_ROW)) & ((1u<<BITS_PER_ROW)-1u);
        dist += (field > r) ? (field - r) : (r - field);
    }
    return dist;
}
uint activeAxes(uint M) {                 // liczba wierszy != tozsamosc
    uint m = 0u;
    for (uint r = 0u; r < uint(N); r++)
        if (((M >> (r*BITS_PER_ROW)) & ((1u<<BITS_PER_ROW)-1u)) != r) m++;
    return m;
}
uint cubieState(uint M) {                 // ruchy-do-ulozenia (dominant) + L1 (tiebreak)
    return activeAxes(M) * (uint(MAX_CUBIE_L1) + 1u) + cubieL1(M);
}''')
t('body', 'Kubik o m aktywnych osiach wymaga do ulozenia okolo m−1 ruchow (drzewo spinajace obrotow Givensa nad jego aktywnymi osiami), wiec m jest bezposrednia miara liczby ruchow. Wazenie go ponad caly zakres L1 sprawia, ze szukanie najpierw minimalizuje **liczbe** ruchow, a dopiero w jej ramach — surowa odleglosc orientacji. To daje scisle monotoniczny gradient w przestrzeni ruchow, ktorego samo L1 nie zapewnia.')

t('h2', '5.3 Skladowe fitnessu i przewazanie koncowki')
t('body', 'Fitness stanu (po danym prefiksie ruchow) laczy dwie czesci: **blad aktywnego klastra** — suma po kubikach klastra `(maxClusterState + cubieState)/max_fA`, gdzie `maxClusterState = MAX_CUBIE_STATE·countActive`, `max_fA = maxClusterState·(countActive+1)` — oraz **naruszenia ulozonych**: liczba kubikow ze zbioru SolvedCubies, ktore przestaly byc ulozone (kazdy dodaje calkowite 1). Poniewaz `MAX_CUBIE_STATE` przewyzsza osiagalne maksimum, czlon aktywny pozostaje scisle < 1, a kazde naruszenie ulozonego kubika (wartosc calkowita) zawsze nad nim dominuje — chroni to juz ulozone klastry.')
t('body', '**Przewazanie koncowki (anty-mono-twist).** Zmniejszanie liczby nieulozonych kubikow jest dobrym drogowskazem na poczatku, ale mylacym pod koniec: konfiguracja z bardzo malo nieulozonymi nie jest latwiejsza, a w 4D i wyzej pojedynczy kubik moze pozostac skrecony w izolacji (mono-twist), z czego bardzo trudno uciec. Gdy liczba nieulozonych aktywnych kubikow spadnie do N lub mniej, blad aktywny mnozymy przez `N/scrambled` — czlon licznosci staje sie staly, a szukanie przestaje gonic za mniejsza liczba kubikow i minimalizuje wzmocniona magnitude orientacji. To przelaczenie jest niezbedne dla N > 3.')

t('h2', '5.4 Kara martwego ruchu (no-op)')
t('body', 'W minimum lokalnym fitness nagradza "nic-nie-rob" (ocena = cube.Score to najmniejsza osiagalna), wiec populacja zbiega do osobnikow, ktorych wypadkowy ruch jest tozsamoscia — best "nic nie robi". Aby temu zapobiec, ewaluator **karze prefiks, ktory nie zmienil aktywnego klastra**. Detekcja jest niemal darmowa: porownanie spakowanej orientacji kazdego aktywnego kubika ze stanem startowym (buforem Cubies).')
t('code', '''bool changed = false;
for (uint i = 0; i < countActive; i++) {
    uint cur = local_cubies[ActiveCubies[i]];
    if (cur != Cubies[ActiveCubies[i]]) changed = true;   // realnie ruszyl klaster?
    float e = GetActiveCubieError(cur, maxClusterState, max_fA);
    local_fA_sum += e; if (e != 0.0) scrambled++;
}
float current = float(local_solved_errors) + local_fA_sum;
if (!changed) current += 1e6;             // no-op na klastrze nie jest rozwiazaniem''')
t('body', 'To poprawne i bezpieczne: prefiks pozostawiajacy klaster nietkniety ma fitness ≥ cube.Score (nigdy nie poprawia), wiec kara nic wartosciowego nie odrzuca. W efekcie minimum ewaluatora przeskakuje z martwego ruchu na **najmniej-zly realny ruch zmieniajacy klaster**. Przewaga nad porownywaniem samego fitnessu jest istotna: na plateau (fitness plaski, ale uklad sie zmienia) porownanie fitnessu falszywie widzialoby "brak zmiany", a porownanie orientacji widzi realny ruch i pozwala kopnac dokladnie tam, gdzie jestesmy zakleszczeni. W macro-ewaluatorze flaga `changed` jest redukowana przez blok (OR).')

# ---- 6 ----
t('h1', '6. Selekcja, krzyzowanie, sortowanie, seedowanie')
t('h2', '6.1 Sortowanie bitoniczne z kara unikalnosci')
t('body', 'Populacja jest sortowana rosnaco wzgledem fitnessu siecia bitoniczna (POPULATION_COUNT jest potega 2). Zbiegajaca populacja szybko zapelnia sie klonami o rownym fitnessie, co zweza pule rodzicow i prowadzi do przedwczesnej zbieznosci. Zamiast osobnego przebiegu deduplikacji, **kara unikalnosci wpieta jest wprost w porownanie**: gdy porownanie znajduje dwa osobniki o rownym fitnessie, jeden dostaje kare rowna maksymalnemu fitnessowi (CUBIES_COUNT). Osobniki o roznym fitnessie wyplywaja na gore, duplikaty tona poza pule zwyciezcow. Poniewaz kara tylko zwieksza fitness, globalne minimum nigdy nie jest karane i indeks 0 pozostaje prawdziwym najlepszym; kara jest przejsciowa (nadpisywana przy nastepnej ewaluacji). Ta jedna zmiana byla decydujaca w praktyce.')

t('h2', '6.2 Selekcja i krzyzowanie (SelCrossover)')
t('body', 'Kazdy watek tworzy jedno dziecko. **Selekcja rankingowa**: dwaj rozni rodzice losowani z gornych WINNERS_RATIO% posortowanej populacji. **Krzyzowanie odwrotno-komplementarne** buduje komutatory — grupowo-teoretyczne narzedzie do przestawiania kilku elementow bez ruszania reszty: pierwsza czesc genomu to split-mix genow obojga rodzicow, a druga polowa to odwrocona sekwencja z zanegowanymi katami (getRevCode). Wynik ma strukture sprzezenia A·B·A⁻¹, z ktorej populacja sklada komutatory 3-cyklu i 2-orientacji domykajace klastry.')

t('h2', '6.3 Makro-mutacja')
t('body', 'Operator mutacji to **nie** losowa zmiana genu (ta jedynie degraduje osobniki i zostala usunieta), lecz makro-mutacja: nadpisanie wiodacych genow dziecka swieza, pelna sekwencja ukladajaca jeden kubik aktywnego klastra, a nastepnie sprzezenie jej fragmentu. Stosowana do frakcji MUTATION_RATIO% dzieci co generacje, nieustannie wstrzykuje do populacji "solwery kubikow", ktore krzyzowanie rekombinuje w rozwiazania wielokubikowe. Bez tego wstrzykiwania material seedowy z inicjalizacji rozmywa sie w ciagu kilku generacji.')

t('h2', '6.4 Seedowanie: generator ruchow cofajacych orientacje')
t('body', 'Zarowno inicjalizacja, jak i makro-mutacja czerpia z podazy sekwencji ukladajacych pojedynczy kubik. Generuje je zachlanne najkrotsze-rozwiazanie losowego aktywnego kubika (`GetSolveSeq`): w kazdym kroku wybieramy losowo ruch (plaszczyzna + kat 90/180/270), ktory obniza RotationCount kubika o jeden, zapisujemy go i aplikujemy — az orientacja stanie sie tozsamoscia. Poniewaz RotationCount jest odlegloscia grafowa do stanu ulozonego, ruch-postep zawsze istnieje na jakiejs najkrotszej sciezce; procedura nigdy sie nie zacina i nie wymaga walidacji. Kazdy ruch realizowany jest z losowa, poprawna osia kolateralna (dowolna spoza plaszczyzny obrotu) — os nie zmienia trajektorii celu, ale roznicuje, ktore inne kubiki sa poruszane przy okazji.')
t('body', 'Host (`BuildSeedMoves`) losuje rozne dekompozycje az do nasycenia puli: przerywa, gdy przez pewien czas nie pojawia sie nowe drzewo (dla N=3 rozne drzewa to czesto ≤3, wiec petla konczy sie po kilkudziesieciu losowaniach zamiast krecic w kolko). Init sieje pierwsze numSeeds osobnikow z tak zebranych sekwencji (SEED_RATIO% populacji jako cel gorny), reszta startuje losowo — realne cisnienie seedujace daje jednak makro-mutacja, nie sam Init.')

# ---- 7 ----
t('h1', '7. Integracja z petla klastrow (host)')
t('body', 'Kostka rozwiazywana jest klaster po klastrze. NextCluster wyznacza kolejny aktywny klaster (kubiki o najmniejszym indeksie klastra, ktore nie sa jeszcze ulozone). Ruchy najlepszego osobnika sa aplikowane na CPU (Turn), a gdy Score spadnie do 0, klaster jest ulozony i przechodzimy do nastepnego.')

t('h2', '7.1 Jedno zrodlo prawdy dla oceny (ScoreCube)')
t('body', 'Baseline `RubikCube.Score` — prog przerwania GA (gdy `best.Fitness < Score`) i akceptacji ciagu ruchow — liczony jest **na GPU** przez kernel `ScoreCube`, tą sama funkcja `scoreState`, ktora realizuja ewaluatory. Wczesniejsze lustrzane obliczenie po stronie CPU (`EvaluateGpu` + pomocnicy) zostalo usuniete: przy kazdej zmianie metryki trzeba bylo synchronizowac shader i host, a rozjazd cichcem psul warunek `best.Fitness < Score`. Teraz metryka zyje w jednym miejscu na GPU; host tylko wgrywa stan kostki, wywoluje dispatch i odczytuje jednego floata z ScoreBuffer.')

t('h2', '7.2 Stall i "kop" — wychodzenie z minimow lokalnych')
t('body', 'Zwykla regula "zastosuj besta tylko gdy poprawia" to czysty zjazd zachlanny, ktory utyka w minimach lokalnych (stad dawny ciezki ogon czasow). Gdy przez `STALL_LIMIT` kolejnych przebiegow GA nic sie nie poprawia, host **stosuje besta mimo braku poprawy** — a poniewaz kara no-op gwarantuje, ze best jest realnym ruchem, jest to prawdziwe szturchniecie wyprowadzajace z kotliny (basin-hopping). Wlaczenie/wylaczenie to jeden wbudowany warunek: `if (best.Fitness < Score || Stall >= STALL_LIMIT)`. Co istotne, kop odpala sie przy **kazdym** minimum lokalnym, nie tylko w globalnej koncowce — a kazdy klaster ma wlasna mini-koncowke (ostatnie sprzezone kubiki), wiec ten sam mechanizm domyka klastry na kazdym etapie, co czyni kostki wieloklastrowe (np. 3^{4}) rozwiazywalnymi.')

t('h2', '7.3 Jedna reprezentacja stanu i cykl zycia buforow')
t('body', 'Stan kostki na CPU trzyma wylacznie Transform (macierz orientacji + pozycja per kubik). Wczesniejsza rownolegla reprezentacja SOA zostala usunieta jako zbedne dublowanie. PackCubies pakuje macierz do formatu shadera wprost z Transform.M (obroty 90° daja dokladne 0/±skala). Bufory tworzone sa raz i reuzywane: `Ssbo.Update` wywoluje `glBufferData`, ktore realokuje magazyn przy zmianie rozmiaru, zachowujac to samo id i binding — eliminuje to churn buforow, typowe zrodlo niestabilnosci sterownika.')

# ---- 8 ----
t('h1', '8. Wyniki')
t('body', 'Solver dochodzi do trudnych konfiguracji w minutach, bez zadnej bazy zapamietanych makro-ruchow. Trzy elementy okazaly sie decydujace i wzajemnie wzmacniajace: metryka ruchow-do-ulozenia z przewazaniem koncowki (rozszerza metode na N > 3), kara unikalnosci wpieta w sort (utrzymuje roznorodnosc), oraz para **kara no-op + kop** (wyprowadza z minimow lokalnych na kazdym etapie).')
t('body', 'Wplyw pary no-op/kop na kostke 2^{4} (jeden sprzezony klaster narozny, 10 ulozen): wzgledem wersji sprzed tej zmiany srednia liczba przebiegow GA spadla z ~27300 do ~3760 (~7×), a ogon z ~136000 do ~15900 (~8,6×); mediana z ~6500 do ~1400. Kostka 6×6×6 uklada sie w okolo 10 minut. Po raz pierwszy ulozona zostala tez pelna 4-wymiarowa kostka **3^{4}** (81 kubikow, wiele typow klastrow) — w okolo 2 minutach i 12055 przebiegach GA.')

# ---- 9 ----
t('h1', '9. Uwagi implementacyjne i pulapki')
t('bullet', '**Jedno zrodlo prawdy**: metryke oceny liczy wylacznie GPU (`scoreState`, uzywane przez ScoreCube i — w formie inline — przez oba ewaluatory). Host nie ma juz lustrzanej kopii, wiec nie ma dryfu CPU↔GPU.')
t('bullet', '**Detekcja no-op po orientacji, nie po fitnessie**: na plateau fitness jest plaski, wiec tylko porownanie spakowanej macierzy poprawnie odroznia ruch boczny (zmieniajacy uklad) od martwego.')
t('bullet', '**Reinterpretacja fitnessu**: GPU zapisuje floatBitsToUint(fitness), host odczytuje bitowo. Sortowanie bitoniczne dziala na wzorcu bitowym (poprawne dla fitnessu ≥ 0).')
t('bullet', '**Licznosci klastra jako uniformy**: countSolved/countActive z hosta, nie z `.length()` bufora — pierwszy klaster ma pusty SolvedCubies, a `.length()` na SSBO rozmiaru 0 jest niepewne miedzy sterownikami.')
t('bullet', '**Wyrownanie std140**: tablica `ivec2 Planes[]` w UBO ma kazdy element wyrownany do 16 bajtow (vec4), wiec host uploaduje po 4 inty na element.')
t('bullet', '**Obejscie bledu sterownika**: w getStartCoordinate ogolny wzor musi lezec w bloku else. Wariant z wczesnym return po `if (SIZE==2)` byl miscompilowany (inline do goracej petli), co dawalo Access Violation zalezny od danych.')
t('space', 6)
t('meta', 'Podsumowanie: potok GPU-GA oddziela wspoldzielone obliczenia (klasa Gpu) od renderowania per-okno. Spakowana macierz w jednym uint pozwala symulowac ruchy w rejestrach; metryka ruchow-do-ulozenia z przewazaniem koncowki daje gladki, monotoniczny krajobraz; kara martwego ruchu plus kop wyprowadzaja z minimow lokalnych; a jedno zrodlo oceny na GPU znosi dryf metryki host-device.')

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
from pdfgen import render

B = []
def t(k, *a): B.append((k,) + a)

t('space', 10)
t('title', "Solving the Full N-Dimensional Rubik's Supercube on the GPU with a Seeded Genetic Algorithm")
t('space', 6)
t('auth', 'Robert Swita, Mateusz Kosikowski, Zbigniew Suszynski')
t('affil', 'Faculty of Electronics and Computer Science, Koszalin University of Technology')
t('affil', 'Department of Multimedia Systems and Artificial Intelligence')
t('space', 8)
t('h2', 'Abstract')
t('abstract', "We present a method for solving the full N-dimensional Rubik's supercube — a Size^{N} hypercube of cubies, each carrying its own orientation, including the internal ones — with a genetic algorithm executed entirely on the GPU as OpenGL compute shaders. Building on a matrix formalization in which cubie orientation is an N-dimensional affine transform decomposed into Euler angles by QR factorization with Givens rotations, we contribute the following. First, a moves-to-solve fitness that augments the L1 orientation distance with the number of active axes of each cubie, together with an endgame reweighting that removes the mono-twist trap dominant for N > 3. Second, GPU-native genetic operators: a reverse-complement (commutator) crossover and a macro-mutation that re-injects per-cubie solving sequences every generation. Third, a diversity-preserving unique selection folded into the bitonic sort. Fourth, a reject-free greedy generator of per-cubie solving sequences that covers every move-reachable decomposition tree. Fifth, a near-free dead-move penalty — a gene prefix that leaves the active cluster unchanged is rejected by comparing packed orientations rather than fitness — which, paired with a stall-driven perturbation that reapplies the least-worsening real move, escapes the local minima that produce the heavy runtime tail. The fitness is computed by a single source of truth on the device. The solver orders clusters from the centre outward and reaches configurations such as the 6x6x6 cube in minutes, and the full four-dimensional 3^{4} cube in about two minutes, without any precomputed macro-move database.")
t('body', '**Keywords:** N-dimensional Rubik\'s cube, genetic algorithm, GPU compute shaders, Givens rotations, group theory, combinatorial optimization, iterated local search.')

t('h1', '1. Introduction')
t('body', "The Rubik's cube, invented in 1974, is one of the best-known combinatorial puzzles; the classic 3x3x3 admits about 4.3x10^{19} configurations. In the N-dimensional generalization the cube becomes a hypercube of Size^{N} cubies, and rotations no longer occur about axes but in two-dimensional planes spanned by pairs of coordinate axes. The number of such planes is N(N-1)/2 — three for 3D, six for 4D, ten for 5D. In previous work the authors solved the full 3D supercube (accounting for the orientation of every cubie, including the interior) with a genetic algorithm that arranges the cube in stages, from the centre outward, restricting moves to an active cluster [1].")
t('body', 'This paper generalizes that approach to arbitrary N >= 3 and moves the entire search onto the graphics processor. The evaluation of a population is embarrassingly parallel: each of POPULATION individuals independently applies GENES moves to CUBIES cubies. A whole generation — initialization, evaluation, sorting and reproduction — runs without returning to the host. The contributions are:')
t('bullet', 'a formalization of the N-dimensional move set and cubie orientation as packed signed-permutation matrices, with a fitness based on the true number of moves needed to solve each cubie (Section 3.1);')
t('bullet', 'an endgame reweighting that prevents the search from stalling on a single badly-oriented cubie (a mono-twist), a failure mode prevalent for N > 3 (Section 3.2);')
t('bullet', 'GPU-native genetic operators: a commutator crossover, a re-injecting macro-mutation, and a unique selection embedded in the bitonic sort (Sections 3.3-3.5);')
t('bullet', 'a reject-free greedy procedure that generates diverse per-cubie solving sequences (seeds) covering every move-reachable decomposition tree (Section 3.6);')
t('bullet', 'a dead-move penalty and a stall-driven perturbation that together escape local minima at every stage of cluster completion (Sections 3.7-3.8).')

t('h1', '2. Formal Model of the N-Dimensional Cube')
t('h2', '2.1 Affine representation of cubies')
t('body', 'An affine transformation in N-dimensional space is a pair T = (M, p) of an N×N matrix and a translation vector, acting as T(x) = Mx + p. Composition of two affine transforms is again affine, with M\' = M_{2}M_{1} and p\' = M_{2}p_{1} + p_{2}. Each cubie is a rigid body described by such a transform. A solved cubie is T = (S, p) with S a diagonal scaling and p its home position. A cube move applies an orthogonal rotation R = (Q, 0) to every cubie of the turned layer, and successive rotations compose into the cubie\'s total transform T\' = (Q\'S, p\'), where Q\' is the accumulated orientation (state) and p\' = Q\'p the current position. Position and orientation are therefore not stored independently: the current position follows from the orientation applied to the home position, so orientation is the only mutable state. A cubie is solved iff its orientation is the identity. Cubies are held in a one-dimensional array indexed by the linear index of their home coordinates; a transformation never changes a cubie\'s slot, only its transform.')

t('h2', '2.2 Orientation as Euler angles by QR decomposition')
t('body', "A rotation in the plane spanned by axes (m, n) is a Givens rotation — the identity except for a 2x2 block [cos, -sin; sin, cos] at the intersections of rows and columns m, n. Any orientation Q' factorizes into a product of such rotations, whose angles — the Euler angles — are the multiples of 90 degrees needed in successive planes. Because the cube's moves are exactly 90-degree rotations, the state is captured by two bits per plane and the whole orientation by a single integer.")
t('body', 'The factorization is obtained by QR decomposition using Givens rotations, which is numerically stable and cheap. Treating the orientation matrix M as input, the algorithm performs P = N(N-1)/2 iterations, each choosing a Givens angle that zeroes one sub-diagonal element, until M is reduced to a diagonal (identity up to sign). The recorded angles define the orientation; reversing them yields a sequence that solves the cubie. The order in which planes are eliminated is a free choice — a strategy — and different orders give different but equally valid factorizations. Since at most N-1 of the P planes carry a non-zero angle, the number of moves required to reach any orientation is bounded by RotationCount <= N-1. The unique orientations of a cubie (orthogonal, determinant +1) number N!·2^{N-1} — 24 for 3D, 192 for 4D, 1920 for 5D — which also bounds the number of cubies in one cluster.')

t('h2', '2.3 Universal move encoding')
t('body', 'An N-dimensional move is defined by four indices: the axis Axis < N perpendicular to the turned layer, the layer Slice < Size along that axis, the rotation plane Plane < N(N-1)/2, and the angle Angle < 3 (90, 180 or 270 degrees), packed into a single integer by linear indexing, Code = ((Axis·Size + Slice)·P + Plane)·3 + Angle, with the constraint that the move axis must differ from both axes of the rotation plane. The total number of legal moves is N·Size·(N-1)·3, so not every code in the range is valid — and, notably, no code denotes the identity: every gene is a real turn. This density is used by the dead-move penalty of Section 3.7.')

t('h2', '2.4 Clusters')
t('body', 'A cluster is the orbit of a cubie under the group of moves that affect it; all cubies sharing a cluster index (the linear index of the sorted magnitudes of their coordinates) belong to one cluster. The solver picks the unsolved cubie nearest the cube centre in the max metric as the active cubie, forms its cluster, restricts the search to the moves affecting that cluster (the free moves), solves it, and repeats outward until the whole cube is arranged. Sequences that finish a cluster can be remembered as reusable macro-moves; the method here needs no such database.')

t('h1', '3. Genetic Algorithm')
t('body', 'A chromosome is a fixed-length sequence of GENES encoded moves, restricted to the free moves of the active cluster, so every individual is a candidate manoeuvre acting only where allowed. The algorithm evolves POPULATION individuals for GENERATIONS generations per invocation, invoked once per cluster attempt.')

t('h2', '3.1 Fitness by number of moves to solve')
t('body', 'Evaluation applies the moves one by one and keeps the best prefix: the number of leading moves that yields the lowest error, with that error. The error separates two groups. The solved group holds cubies from finished clusters that must not be disturbed; each violated one adds a whole unit. The active group holds the current cluster; for an active cubie we define a per-cubie penalty, zero iff solved and otherwise dominated by how many moves it still needs:')
t('bodyc', 'cubieState(M) = m · (MAX_CUBIE_L1 + 1) + L_{1}(M),')
t('body', 'where m is the number of active axes (rows of the packed matrix differing from the identity) and L_{1} is the Manhattan distance of the packed orientation from the identity. A cubie with active-axis count m needs about m-1 moves to solve (a spanning tree of Givens rotations over its active axes), so m is a direct moves-to-solve measure; weighting it above the entire L1 range makes the search minimise the number of moves first and refine the raw distance only within that — a strictly monotone gradient in move space that L1 alone does not provide. The cluster error is the normalized sum ( Sum_active (maxClusterState + cubieState) ) / max_fA + Sum_solved 1, with maxClusterState = MAX_CUBIE_STATE·|A|, max_fA = maxClusterState·(|A|+1), so the active term stays strictly below one and the integer count of disturbed solved cubies always dominates it.')

t('h2', '3.2 Endgame reweighting against the mono-twist')
t('body', 'Reducing the count of unsolved cubies guides well early but misleads near the end: a configuration with very few unsolved cubies is not necessarily easier, and in 4D and higher a single cubie can remain twisted in isolation — a mono-twist — which is very hard to escape (unlike 3D, where the orientation-sum invariant forbids a lone twist, the non-abelian 4D orientation group admits it). We therefore switch the objective once the number of unsolved active cubies falls to N or fewer: the active error is multiplied by N/scrambled, where scrambled is that count. The count contribution becomes constant across the endgame, so the search stops chasing fewer cubies and minimises the amplified orientation magnitude; a lone hard cubie receives the maximum penalty (a factor of N). The switch is essential for N > 3.')

t('h2', '3.3 Selection with uniqueness embedded in the sort')
t('body', 'The population is sorted by fitness with a bitonic network, the fittest at index 0; parents are drawn by rank from the top WINNERS fraction. A converging population quickly fills with equal-fitness clones, collapsing the parent pool. Rather than a separate deduplication pass, a unique selection is folded into the sort: whenever the compare-and-exchange finds two equal-fitness individuals, one is demoted by a penalty equal to the maximum possible fitness (CUBIES). Distinct-fitness individuals rise while duplicates sink out of the winner pool. Because the penalty only increases fitness, the global minimum is never penalised and index 0 remains a true best; the penalty is transient, overwritten by the next evaluation. This single change was decisive in practice.')

t('h2', '3.4 Crossover')
t('body', "Reproduction uses a reverse-complement crossover that builds commutators — the group-theoretic tool for permuting a few pieces without disturbing the rest. A child inherits a prefix from one parent and a middle block from the other; the second half of the chromosome is then the first half reversed and inverted (each move's angle negated). The result has the structure of a conjugate A·B·A^{-1}, from which the population assembles the 3-cycle and 2-orientation commutators that finish clusters.")

t('h2', '3.5 Macro-mutation')
t('body', 'The mutation operator is not a random gene change — which only degrades individuals — but a macro-mutation that overwrites the leading genes of a child with a fresh, complete sequence solving one active-cluster cubie, then conjugates a block of it. Applied to a fraction MUTATION of the children every generation, it continually re-injects cubie-solvers, which crossover recombines into multi-cubie solutions. Without this re-injection the seed material from initialization is diluted away within a few generations.')

t('h2', '3.6 Seed generation by greedy shortest-solve')
t('body', "Both the initial seeding and the macro-mutation draw on a supply of per-cubie solving sequences, generated by a greedy shortest-solve of a random active cubie: at each step pick, uniformly at random, a cube move (a plane and a 90/180/270-degree angle) that lowers the cubie's RotationCount by one, record it, apply it, until the orientation is the identity. Because RotationCount is the graph distance to the solved state, a progress move always exists on some shortest path, so the procedure never gets stuck and needs no validation. Each move is realized by choosing any axis not in its rotation plane and reading the cubie's current layer along that axis; the plane rotation is applied regardless of the chosen axis, so the target's trajectory is axis-independent while the axis varies which other cubies are collaterally disturbed — an orthogonal, cheap source of diversity.")
t('body', "A combinatorial analysis over all reachable orientations confirms that this greedy generator covers every decomposition tree reachable by cube moves. For a fully-scrambled 4D cubie, the shortest solutions use N-1 = 3 rotation planes; counting distinct plane-sets yields 12 spanning trees, while counting distinct ordered sequences yields 16 (the extra four are non-commuting reorderings of the same plane-set). The RotationCount-driven greedy reaches all 16 ordered decompositions (12 sets), whereas the lighter variant below covers 12 of 16 (10 of 12 sets). We note that RotationCount is an order-dependent QR count, not a geometric distance, which is why a move touching an already-solved axis can still lower it; the greedy nonetheless remains reject-free over all reachable states up to 5D.")
t('code', '''while (RotationCount(cubie) > 0):
    cand = [ (plane, angle) for all planes, angles in {90,180,270}
             if RotationCountAfter(cubie, plane, angle) == RotationCount - 1 ]
    (plane, angle) = random choice from cand   # every choice is on a shortest path
    axis  = any axis not in plane              # collateral-diversity dimension
    slice = cubie.coordinate(axis)             # layer currently holding the cubie
    emit Encode(axis, slice, plane, angle); apply the move to the cubie''')
t('body', 'The host draws distinct decompositions until the pool saturates (it stops after a run with no new tree; for N = 3 the distinct trees are often three or fewer, so the loop ends quickly instead of spinning). A lighter variant replaces RotationCount with the number of non-positive diagonal entries of the orientation matrix — read directly, no decomposition — likewise never stuck and covering 10 of the 12 trees.')

t('h2', '3.7 Dead-move penalty')
t('body', "In a local minimum the fitness rewards doing nothing — the baseline score is the smallest attainable — so the population converges to individuals whose net move is the identity, and the best returned by a generation does nothing. To prevent this, the evaluator penalizes a gene prefix that leaves the active cluster unchanged, detected almost for free by comparing each active cubie's packed orientation against the starting state:")
t('code', '''bool changed = false;
for i in active:
    cur = cube[ActiveCubies[i]]
    if (cur != Cubies[ActiveCubies[i]]) changed = true   # did the prefix move the cluster?
    ... accumulate error ...
if (!changed) fitness += LARGE     # a no-op on the active cluster is not a solution''')
t('body', 'This is safe: a prefix leaving the cluster untouched has fitness at least the baseline (it never improves), so the penalty discards nothing useful. Its advantage over a fitness-based check is decisive on a plateau — where the fitness is flat but the arrangement genuinely changes — because comparing fitness would falsely report "no change" exactly where the search is stuck, whereas comparing orientation sees the real move. With this penalty the per-generation best is always a real cluster-changing move; in the endgame, the least-worsening one.')

t('h2', '3.8 Stall-driven perturbation')
t('body', 'The plain rule of applying the best only when it improves is pure greedy descent, which stalls in local minima and produces a heavy-tailed runtime distribution. When no improvement occurs for STALL consecutive invocations, the host applies the best regardless — and because the dead-move penalty guarantees a real move, this is a genuine perturbation that escapes the basin (an iterated-local-search kick). The trigger is a single condition, best.Fitness < Score OR Stall >= STALL. Crucially the kick fires at every local minimum, not only the global endgame; since every cluster has its own coupled mini-endgame, the same mechanism completes clusters at each stage, which is what makes multi-cluster cubes such as the 3^{4} tractable.')

t('h1', '4. GPU Implementation')
t('h2', '4.1 Compute-shader pipeline')
t('body', 'The algorithm runs as OpenGL compute programs sharing storage buffers. Per generation the host issues: (1) evaluate the parent population, writing each best-prefix fitness (with the dead-move penalty); (2) a bitonic sort with the uniqueness penalty; (3) read back the best and stop early if it beats the current baseline; (4) selection, crossover and macro-mutation, writing children into a second buffer. The two population buffers are ping-pong: parents at binding 0, children at binding 1, roles swapped after each generation. Only the best individual is read back per generation; all heavy work stays on the device.')

t('h2', '4.2 Packed orientation')
t('body', "A cubie's orientation is a signed permutation matrix — exactly one non-zero entry, +1 or -1, per row and column — packed into one 32-bit integer: N rows of BITS_PER_ROW bits, each holding the column index of its non-zero entry (BITS_FOR_COL = 2 for N <= 4, else 3) plus one sign bit. The identity row r encodes the value r, so a solved cubie packs to a fixed constant and a single 32-bit integer suffices up to eight dimensions. Applying a move is pure bit manipulation of two rows; the L1 distance and active-axis count are read off directly.")

t('h2', '4.3 Buffers, single-source scoring, parallel evaluation')
t('body', 'Compile-time constants (dimension, size, population, genes) are injected into the shader source as preprocessor defines, since they size fixed arrays; the shaders are recompiled when the cube dimension or size changes. Cluster sizes are passed as uniforms, not read from buffer lengths, since a first cluster has an empty solved-set and a zero-size buffer length is unreliable across drivers. Two evaluation kernels are provided: a micro kernel (one thread per individual, cube in registers) for small cubes, and a macro kernel (one thread block per individual, cube in shared memory, error summed by a logarithmic parallel reduction) for larger ones.')
t('body', 'Crucially, the acceptance baseline is computed by a single source of truth on the device: a one-thread ScoreCube kernel scores the current cube with the same scoreState function the evaluators use, and the host reads back one float. An earlier host-side mirror of the metric was removed — keeping two copies in sync across the CPU and the shader was a recurring source of silent drift in the best.Fitness < Score test. The buffer layout is summarized in Table 1.')
t('table', [
    ['Binding', 'Buffer', 'Contents'],
    ['0', 'Population', 'Parent individuals (fitness, best-prefix length, genes)'],
    ['1', 'NewPopulation', 'Children written by crossover (ping-pong)'],
    ['2', 'Cubies', 'Packed starting orientation, one uint per cubie (shared)'],
    ['3', 'FreeMoves', 'Legal move codes for the active cluster'],
    ['4', 'SolvedCubies', 'Home indices of already-solved cubies'],
    ['5', 'ActiveCubies', 'Home indices of the active cluster'],
    ['6', 'Planes (UBO)', 'Axis pairs of the rotation planes'],
    ['7', 'SeedMoves', 'Per-individual solving sequences (initialization / mutation)'],
    ['8', 'ScoreBuffer', 'Baseline cube score written by the ScoreCube kernel'],
], [46, 82, 300])
t('cap', 'Table 1. Storage-buffer registry shared by the compute programs.')

t('h1', '5. Results and Discussion')
t('body', 'The solver arranges the cube cluster by cluster from the centre outward, driven only by the generated seeds, crossover, macro-mutation, the sort-embedded unique selection, and the dead-move/stall pair — with no stored macro-move database. In this configuration it solves the 6x6x6 cube in about ten minutes, and finishes clusters at least as quickly as the previous CPU solver. It also solves, for the first time, the full four-dimensional 3^{4} cube (81 cubies, several cluster types) in about two minutes and roughly 12000 algorithm invocations.')
t('body', 'The dead-move penalty and the stall perturbation are together responsible for the largest reduction of the heavy runtime tail. On the 2^{4} cube — a single coupled cluster of corner cubies, the hardest single-cluster case — the mean number of algorithm invocations dropped from about 27000 to about 3800 (~7x) and the worst case from about 136000 to about 16000 (~8.6x), with the median falling from about 6500 to about 1400, relative to the version before this change. The other decisive, mutually reinforcing elements are the macro-mutation (without which the seeds vanish after the first generation) and the sort-embedded unique selection (which produced the qualitative jump from "stuck" to reliable cluster completion).')
t('body', 'The fitness is now computed by one function on the device and read back for the acceptance baseline, removing the earlier host/device duplication; a bit-exact cross-check between a CPU port of the move kernel and the shader was used during development to guarantee that the packed simulation matches the reference. Because the costly per-candidate decomposition in seed generation runs only once per invocation, its cost is negligible against the evolutionary loop; where it is not, the diagonal-count metric of Section 3.6 removes the decomposition entirely at the price of two decomposition trees. The compute path scales with the population and cube size and is bounded by device memory for the packed representation, which grows only linearly in the number of cubies.')

t('h1', '6. Conclusions')
t('body', "We generalized a staged, cluster-by-cluster genetic solver of the full Rubik's supercube to arbitrary dimension and executed it entirely on the GPU. The key ideas are a fitness that measures the true number of moves to solve each cubie (with an endgame reweighting that defeats the mono-twist), genetic operators that build commutators and continually re-inject cubie-solving sequences, a unique selection folded into the sort, a reject-free greedy generator of seeds covering every move-reachable decomposition tree, and — decisive for the runtime tail — a near-free dead-move penalty paired with a stall-driven perturbation that escapes local minima at every stage, all scored by a single source of truth on the device. Together they solve high-dimensional cubes within minutes without a macro-move database. Future work includes exploiting the symmetry of the hypercube to shrink the search space, learning and reusing cluster-finishing macros across cube sizes, and replacing the legacy immediate-mode display with a retained-mode renderer.")

t('h1', 'References')
t('body', "[1] R. Swita, Z. Suszynski. Solving Full NxNxN Rubik's Supercube Using a Genetic Algorithm. International Journal of Computer Games Technology, vol. 2023, art. 2445335, 2023.")
t('body', "[2] T. Rokicki, H. Kociemba, M. Davidson, J. Dethridge. The Diameter of the Rubik's Cube Group Is Twenty. SIAM J. Discrete Math., 27(2):1082-1105, 2013.")
t('body', "[3] E. Demaine, M. Demaine, S. Eisenstat, A. Lubiw, A. Winslow. Algorithms for Solving Rubik's Cubes. In ESA 2011, LNCS 6942, pp. 689-700, Springer, 2011.")
t('body', "[4] R. E. Korf. Finding Optimal Solutions to Rubik's Cube Using Pattern Databases. In AAAI-97, pp. 700-705, 1997.")
t('body', "[5] F. Agostinelli, S. McAleer, A. Shmakov, P. Baldi. Solving the Rubik's Cube with Deep Reinforcement Learning and Search. Nature Machine Intelligence, 1:356-363, 2019.")
t('body', "[6] N. El-Sourani, S. Hauke, M. Borschbach. An Evolutionary Approach for Solving the Rubik's Cube Incorporating Exact Methods. In EvoApplications 2010, LNCS 6024, pp. 80-89, Springer, 2010.")
t('body', "[7] M. Luby, A. Sinclair, D. Zuckerman. Optimal Speedup of Las Vegas Algorithms. Information Processing Letters, 47(4):173-180, 1993.")
t('body', "[8] G. H. Golub, C. F. Van Loan. Matrix Computations, 3rd ed. Johns Hopkins University Press, 1996.")

Any orientation Q' factorizes into a product of such rotations, whose angles — the Euler angles — are the multiples of 90 degrees needed in successive planes. Because the cube's moves are exactly 90-degree rotations, the state is captured by two bits per plane and the whole orientation by a single integer.")
t('body', 'The factorization is obtained by QR decomposition using Givens rotations, which is numerically stable and cheap. Treating the orientation matrix M as input, the algorithm performs P = N(N-1)/2 iterations, each choosing a Givens angle that zeroes one sub-diagonal element, until M is reduced to a diagonal (identity up to sign). The recorded angles define the orientation; reversing them yields a sequence that solves the cubie. The order in which planes are eliminated is a free choice — a strategy — and different orders give different but equally valid factorizations. Since at most N-1 of the P planes carry a non-zero angle, the number of moves required to reach any orientation is bounded by RotationCount <= N-1. The unique orientations of a cubie (orthogonal, determinant +1) number N!·2^{N-1} — 24 for 3D, 192 for 4D, 1920 for 5D — which also bounds the number of cubies in one cluster.')

t('h2', '2.3 Universal move encoding')
t('body', 'An N-dimensional move is defined by four indices: the axis Axis < N perpendicular to the turned layer, the layer Slice < Size along that axis, the rotation plane Plane < N(N-1)/2, and the angle Angle < 3 (90, 180 or 270 degrees), packed into a single integer by linear indexing, Code = ((Axis·Size + Slice)·P + Plane)·3 + Angle, with the constraint that the move axis must differ from both axes of the rotation plane. The total number of legal moves is N·Size·(N-1)·3, so not every code in the range is valid — and, notably, no code denotes the identity: every gene is a real turn. This density is used by the dead-move penalty of Section 3.7.')

t('h2', '2.4 Clusters')
t('body', 'A cluster is the orbit of a cubie under the group of moves that affect it; all cubies sharing a cluster index (the linear index of the sorted magnitudes of their coordinates) belong to one cluster. The solver picks the unsolved cubie nearest the cube centre in the max metric as the active cubie, forms its cluster, restricts the search to the moves affecting that cluster (the free moves), solves it, and repeats outward until the whole cube is arranged. Sequences that finish a cluster can be remembered as reusable macro-moves; the method here needs no such database.')

t('h1', '3. Genetic Algorithm')
t('body', 'A chromosome is a fixed-length sequence of GENES encoded moves, restricted to the free moves of the active cluster, so every individual is a candidate manoeuvre acting only where allowed. The algorithm evolves POPULATION individuals for GENERATIONS generations per invocation, invoked once per cluster attempt.')

t('h2', '3.1 Fitness by number of moves to solve')
t('body', 'Evaluation applies the moves one by one and keeps the best prefix: the number of leading moves that yields the lowest error, with that error. The error separates two groups. The solved group holds cubies from finished clusters that must not be disturbed; each violated one adds a whole unit. The active group holds the current cluster; for an active cubie we define a per-cubie penalty, zero iff solved and otherwise dominated by how many moves it still needs:')
t('bodyc', 'cubieState(M) = m · (MAX_CUBIE_L1 + 1) + L_{1}(M),')
t('body', 'where m is the number of active axes (rows of the packed matrix differing from the identity) and L_{1} is the Manhattan distance of the packed orientation from the identity. A cubie with active-axis count m needs about m-1 moves to solve (a spanning tree of Givens rotations over its active axes), so m is a direct moves-to-solve measure; weighting it above the entire L1 range makes the search minimise the number of moves first and refine the raw distance only within that — a strictly monotone gradient in move space that L1 alone does not provide. The cluster error is the normalized sum ( Sum_active (maxClusterState + cubieState) ) / max_fA + Sum_solved 1, with maxClusterState = MAX_CUBIE_STATE·|A|, max_fA = maxClusterState·(|A|+1), so the active term stays strictly below one and the integer count of disturbed solved cubies always dominates it.')

t('h2', '3.2 Endgame reweighting against the mono-twist')
t('body', 'Reducing the count of unsolved cubies guides well early but misleads near the end: a configuration with very few unsolved cubies is not necessarily easier, and in 4D and higher a single cubie can remain twisted in isolation — a mono-twist — which is very hard to escape (unlike 3D, where the orientation-sum invariant forbids a lone twist, the non-abelian 4D orientation group admits it). We therefore switch the objective once the number of unsolved active cubies falls to N or fewer: the active error is multiplied by N/scrambled, where scrambled is that count. The count contribution becomes constant across the endgame, so the search stops chasing fewer cubies and minimises the amplified orientation magnitude; a lone hard cubie receives the maximum penalty (a factor of N). The switch is essential for N > 3.')

t('h2', '3.3 Selection with uniqueness embedded in the sort')
t('body', 'The population is sorted by fitness with a bitonic network, the fittest at index 0; parents are drawn by rank from the top WINNERS fraction. A converging population quickly fills with equal-fitness clones, collapsing the parent pool. Rather than a separate deduplication pass, a unique selection is folded into the sort: whenever the compare-and-exchange finds two equal-fitness individuals, one is demoted by a penalty equal to the maximum possible fitness (CUBIES). Distinct-fitness individuals rise while duplicates sink out of the winner pool. Because the penalty only increases fitness, the global minimum is never penalised and index 0 remains a true best; the penalty is transient, overwritten by the next evaluation. This single change was decisive in practice.')

t('h2', '3.4 Crossover')
t('body', "Reproduction uses a reverse-complement crossover that builds commutators — the group-theoretic tool for permuting a few pieces without disturbing the rest. A child inherits a prefix from one parent and a middle block from the other; the second half of the chromosome is then the first half reversed and inverted (each move's angle negated). The result has the structure of a conjugate A·B·A^{-1}, from which the population assembles the 3-cycle and 2-orientation commutators that finish clusters.")

t('h2', '3.5 Macro-mutation')
t('body', 'The mutation operator is not a random gene change — which only degrades individuals — but a macro-mutation that overwrites the leading genes of a child with a fresh, complete sequence solving one active-cluster cubie, then conjugates a block of it. Applied to a fraction MUTATION of the children every generation, it continually re-injects cubie-solvers, which crossover recombines into multi-cubie solutions. Without this re-injection the seed material from initialization is diluted away within a few generations.')

t('h2', '3.6 Seed generation by greedy shortest-solve')
t('body', "Both the initial seeding and the macro-mutation draw on a supply of per-cubie solving sequences, generated by a greedy shortest-solve of a random active cubie: at each step pick, uniformly at random, a cube move (a plane and a 90/180/270-degree angle) that lowers the cubie's RotationCount by one, record it, apply it, until the orientation is the identity. Because RotationCount is the graph distance to the solved state, a progress move always exists on some shortest path, so the procedure never gets stuck and needs no validation. Each move is realized by choosing any axis not in its rotation plane and reading the cubie's current layer along that axis; the plane rotation is applied regardless of the chosen axis, so the target's trajectory is axis-independent while the axis varies which other cubies are collaterally disturbed — an orthogonal, cheap source of diversity.")
t('body', "A combinatorial analysis over all reachable orientations confirms that this greedy generator covers every decomposition tree reachable by cube moves. For a fully-scrambled 4D cubie, the shortest solutions use N-1 = 3 rotation planes; counting distinct plane-sets yields 12 spanning trees, while counting distinct ordered sequences yields 16 (the extra four are non-commuting reorderings of the same plane-set). The RotationCount-driven greedy reaches all 16 ordered decompositions (12 sets), whereas the lighter variant below covers 12 of 16 (10 of 12 sets). We note that RotationCount is an order-dependent QR count, not a geometric distance, which is why a move touching an already-solved axis can still lower it; the greedy nonetheless remains reject-free over all reachable states up to 5D.")
t('code', '''while (RotationCount(cubie) > 0):
    cand = [ (plane, angle) for all planes, angles in {90,180,270}
             if RotationCountAfter(cubie, plane, angle) == RotationCount - 1 ]
    (plane, angle) = random choice from cand   # every choice is on a shortest path
    axis  = any axis not in plane              # collateral-diversity dimension
    slice = cubie.coordinate(axis)             # layer currently holding the cubie
    emit Encode(axis, slice, plane, angle); apply the move to the cubie''')
t('body', 'The host draws distinct decompositions until the pool saturates (it stops after a run with no new tree; for N = 3 the distinct trees are often three or fewer, so the loop ends quickly instead of spinning). A lighter variant replaces RotationCount with the number of non-positive diagonal entries of the orientation matrix — read directly, no decomposition — likewise never stuck and covering 10 of the 12 trees.')

t('h2', '3.7 Dead-move penalty')
t('body', "In a local minimum the fitness rewards doing nothing — the baseline score is the smallest attainable — so the population converges to individuals whose net move is the identity, and the best returned by a generation does nothing. To prevent this, the evaluator penalizes a gene prefix that leaves the active cluster unchanged, detected almost for free by comparing each active cubie's packed orientation against the starting state:")
t('code', '''bool changed = false;
for i in active:
    cur = cube[ActiveCubies[i]]
    if (cur != Cubies[ActiveCubies[i]]) changed = true   # did the prefix move the cluster?
    ... accumulate error ...
if (!changed) fitness += LARGE     # a no-op on the active cluster is not a solution''')
t('body', 'This is safe: a prefix leaving the cluster untouched has fitness at least the baseline (it never improves), so the penalty discards nothing useful. Its advantage over a fitness-based check is decisive on a plateau — where the fitness is flat but the arrangement genuinely changes — because comparing fitness would falsely report "no change" exactly where the search is stuck, whereas comparing orientation sees the real move. With this penalty the per-generation best is always a real cluster-changing move; in the endgame, the least-worsening one.')

t('h2', '3.8 Stall-driven perturbation')
t('body', 'The plain rule of applying the best only when it improves is pure greedy descent, which stalls in local minima and produces a heavy-tailed runtime distribution. When no improvement occurs for STALL consecutive invocations, the host applies the best regardless — and because the dead-move penalty guarantees a real move, this is a genuine perturbation that escapes the basin (an iterated-local-search kick). The trigger is a single condition, best.Fitness < Score OR Stall >= STALL. Crucially the kick fires at every local minimum, not only the global endgame; since every cluster has its own coupled mini-endgame, the same mechanism completes clusters at each stage, which is what makes multi-cluster cubes such as the 3^{4} tractable.')

t('h1', '4. GPU Implementation')
t('h2', '4.1 Compute-shader pipeline')
t('body', 'The algorithm runs as OpenGL compute programs sharing storage buffers. Per generation the host issues: (1) evaluate the parent population, writing each best-prefix fitness (with the dead-move penalty); (2) a bitonic sort with the uniqueness penalty; (3) read back the best and stop early if it beats the current baseline; (4) selection, crossover and macro-mutation, writing children into a second buffer. The two population buffers are ping-pong: parents at binding 0, children at binding 1, roles swapped after each generation. Only the best individual is read back per generation; all heavy work stays on the device.')

t('h2', '4.2 Packed orientation')
t('body', "A cubie's orientation is a signed permutation matrix — exactly one non-zero entry, +1 or -1, per row and column — packed into one 32-bit integer: N rows of BITS_PER_ROW bits, each holding the column index of its non-zero entry (BITS_FOR_COL = 2 for N <= 4, else 3) plus one sign bit. The identity row r encodes the value r, so a solved cubie packs to a fixed constant and a single 32-bit integer suffices up to eight dimensions. Applying a move is pure bit manipulation of two rows; the L1 distance and active-axis count are read off directly.")

t('h2', '4.3 Buffers, single-source scoring, parallel evaluation')
t('body', 'Compile-time constants (dimension, size, population, genes) are injected into the shader source as preprocessor defines, since they size fixed arrays; the shaders are recompiled when the cube dimension or size changes. Cluster sizes are passed as uniforms, not read from buffer lengths, since a first cluster has an empty solved-set and a zero-size buffer length is unreliable across drivers. Two evaluation kernels are provided: a micro kernel (one thread per individual, cube in registers) for small cubes, and a macro kernel (one thread block per individual, cube in shared memory, error summed by a logarithmic parallel reduction) for larger ones.')
t('body', 'Crucially, the acceptance baseline is computed by a single source of truth on the device: a one-thread ScoreCube kernel scores the current cube with the same scoreState function the evaluators use, and the host reads back one float. An earlier host-side mirror of the metric was removed — keeping two copies in sync across the CPU and the shader was a recurring source of silent drift in the best.Fitness < Score test. The buffer layout is summarized in Table 1.')
t('table', [
    ['Binding', 'Buffer', 'Contents'],
    ['0', 'Population', 'Parent individuals (fitness, best-prefix length, genes)'],
    ['1', 'NewPopulation', 'Children written by crossover (ping-pong)'],
    ['2', 'Cubies', 'Packed starting orientation, one uint per cubie (shared)'],
    ['3', 'FreeMoves', 'Legal move codes for the active cluster'],
    ['4', 'SolvedCubies', 'Home indices of already-solved cubies'],
    ['5', 'ActiveCubies', 'Home indices of the active cluster'],
    ['6', 'Planes (UBO)', 'Axis pairs of the rotation planes'],
    ['7', 'SeedMoves', 'Per-individual solving sequences (initialization / mutation)'],
    ['8', 'ScoreBuffer', 'Baseline cube score written by the ScoreCube kernel'],
], [46, 82, 300])
t('cap', 'Table 1. Storage-buffer registry shared by the compute programs.')

t('h1', '5. Results and Discussion')
t('body', 'The solver arranges the cube cluster by cluster from the centre outward, driven only by the generated seeds, crossover, macro-mutation, the sort-embedded unique selection, and the dead-move/stall pair — with no stored macro-move database. In this configuration it solves the 6x6x6 cube in about ten minutes, and finishes clusters at least as quickly as the previous CPU solver. It also solves, for the first time, the full four-dimensional 3^{4} cube (81 cubies, several cluster types) in about two minutes and roughly 12000 algorithm invocations.')
t('body', 'The dead-move penalty and the stall perturbation are together responsible for the largest reduction of the heavy runtime tail. On the 2^{4} cube — a single coupled cluster of corner cubies, the hardest single-cluster case — the mean number of algorithm invocations dropped from about 27000 to about 3800 (~7x) and the worst case from about 136000 to about 16000 (~8.6x), with the median falling from about 6500 to about 1400, relative to the version before this change. The other decisive, mutually reinforcing elements are the macro-mutation (without which the seeds vanish after the first generation) and the sort-embedded unique selection (which produced the qualitative jump from "stuck" to reliable cluster completion).')
t('body', 'The fitness is now computed by one function on the device and read back for the acceptance baseline, removing the earlier host/device duplication; a bit-exact cross-check between a CPU port of the move kernel and the shader was used during development to guarantee that the packed simulation matches the reference. Because the costly per-candidate decomposition in seed generation runs only once per invocation, its cost is negligible against the evolutionary loop; where it is not, the diagonal-count metric of Section 3.6 removes the decomposition entirely at the price of two decomposition trees. The compute path scales with the population and cube size and is bounded by device memory for the packed representation, which grows only linearly in the number of cubies.')

t('h1', '6. Conclusions')
t('body', "We generalized a staged, cluster-by-cluster genetic solver of the full Rubik's supercube to arbitrary dimension and executed it entirely on the GPU. The key ideas are a fitness that measures the true number of moves to solve each cubie (with an endgame reweighting that defeats the mono-twist), genetic operators that build commutators and continually re-inject cubie-solving sequences, a unique selection folded into the sort, a reject-free greedy generator of seeds covering every move-reachable decomposition tree, and — decisive for the runtime tail — a near-free dead-move penalty paired with a stall-driven perturbation that escapes local minima at every stage, all scored by a single source of truth on the device. Together they solve high-dimensional cubes within minutes without a macro-move database. Future work includes exploiting the symmetry of the hypercube to shrink the search space, learning and reusing cluster-finishing macros across cube sizes, and replacing the legacy immediate-mode display with a retained-mode renderer.")
